title: Eligibility Verification
description: Master 270/271 inquiries, active coverage, cost-share math, COB, and prior-auth flags.

questions.q: What is the 270/271 transaction used for?
options: Sending a claim to the payer
Checking a patient's eligibility and benefits
Posting a payment from the payer
Filing an appeal on a denied claim
questions.explanation: The 270 is the eligibility inquiry and the 271 is the payer's response. They are used before the visit to confirm coverage and benefits. Claims travel on the 837, payments come back on the 835, and appeals follow a separate process.
questions.hint: Which transaction happens BEFORE the visit?

questions.q: A patient's coverage shows as active. What does that actually guarantee?
options: The payer will pay for today's visit
Coverage is active, but payment is not guaranteed
No copay or deductible is owed
No prior authorization will ever be needed
questions.explanation: Active coverage only means the plan is in force on that date. Payment still depends on medical necessity, covered services, correct coding, and benefits like deductibles. Active coverage is necessary but never sufficient on its own.
questions.hint: Active coverage answers 'is the plan on?' — not 'will they pay?'

questions.q: The 271 response shows: copay $30, deductible $1,000 (met $200), coinsurance 20%. What is the patient's cost share?
options: Only the $30 copay matters
$30 copay, $800 remaining deductible, then 20% coinsurance
The deductible is already fully met
Coinsurance applies before the deductible
questions.explanation: Cost share stacks in order: the copay is collected at the visit, then the remaining deductible ($1,000 minus $200 met = $800) must be satisfied, and only then does the 20% coinsurance apply to the allowed amount. Getting this order right prevents surprise patient bills.
questions.hint: Deductible comes before coinsurance — do the subtraction.

questions.q: What is COB, and why must it be checked?
options: Coordination of Benefits — it determines which payer is primary when a patient has two plans
Cost of Billing — the fee the clearinghouse charges per claim
Change of Beneficiary — updating the patient's mailing address
Claim Override Batch — a method for resubmitting denied claims
questions.explanation: COB (Coordination of Benefits) establishes the primary payer when a patient carries more than one plan. Billing the wrong payer first causes denials and rework, because the secondary payer only processes a claim after the primary has adjudicated it.
questions.hint: Two insurance cards in the wallet — which one goes first?

questions.q: The 271 response flags 'prior authorization required' for an MRI. What should happen next?
options: Ignore the flag and bill the MRI normally
Obtain authorization from the payer before performing the MRI
Bill the patient for the full MRI cost
Skip the MRI and code a different service instead
questions.explanation: When the payer requires prior authorization, approval must be secured before the service happens, or the claim will deny as non-covered. Billing the patient to dodge it or swapping in different codes is wrong and can cross into fraud.
questions.hint: The word 'prior' tells you the timing.

timeline.details: 270 inquiry sent to payer. 271 response: ACTIVE coverage, $2,500 deductible ($1,800 met), $40 copay for office visits. Prior auth: not required for this service.
CPT 99213 entered with diagnosis. Charge amount: $180. Claim created and scrubbed — 13 rules passed.
Claim accepted by clearinghouse. Forwarded to payer. No rejections — clean claim.
835 ERA received: Billed $180, Allowed $120, Paid $80, Patient responsibility $40 (PR-3 copay). Contractual adjustment: $60 (CO-45).
$40 copay balance moved to patient statement. Statement sent. This is where YOUR training continues — work the A/R!

title: Patient Registration
description: Register a new patient with complete, accurate demographics — the foundation of every clean claim.

questions.q: Which fields are REQUIRED to register a new patient?
options: Full name, date of birth, phone
Only the patient's first name
Email address only
Insurance card number only
questions.explanation: Name, DOB, and phone are the minimum to uniquely identify a patient and contact them. Without DOB you can't verify identity; without phone you can't reach them for scheduling or balances.
questions.hint: What three things identify and reach a patient?

questions.q: A patient's name is spelled 'Jon' on the ID but 'John' in your system. What should you do?
options: Leave it — close enough
Correct it to match the photo ID exactly
Delete the record and start over
Ask the patient to change their ID
questions.explanation: Demographics must match the photo ID exactly. Mismatched names cause eligibility failures (the payer can't find the patient) and claim rejections. Always correct to the ID.
questions.hint: What does the payer match against?

questions.q: Why is the date of birth critical at registration?
options: It determines the patient's copay
It's used for identity verification and eligibility matching
It's only needed for pediatric patients
It sets the appointment length
questions.explanation: DOB is a key identity verifier — payers match name + DOB + member ID. Wrong DOB means the 270 eligibility check fails and the claim denies as CO-16 (missing/invalid information).
questions.hint: Which transaction needs name + DOB?

questions.q: A duplicate patient record is created (same person, two charts). What's the risk?
options: No risk — more records are better
Split clinical history, billing errors, and compliance issues
It speeds up check-in
It lowers the patient's deductible
questions.explanation: Duplicates split the clinical and billing history across two charts — charges go to the wrong record, eligibility checks fail, and it creates HIPAA/compliance risk. Always search before creating.
questions.hint: What happens to the patient's history?

questions.q: When should you verify a returning patient's demographics?
options: Never — they were verified once
At every visit, before the encounter
Only when they complain
Once per year
questions.explanation: Verify at every visit. People move, change numbers, and get new insurance constantly. Stale demographics are the #1 cause of front-end denials — a 30-second check prevents a denied claim.
questions.hint: How often do phone numbers and addresses change?

title: Insurance Verification
description: Read insurance cards, verify active coverage, and spot inactive or terminated plans before the visit.

questions.q: A patient's insurance card shows an effective date of 01/01/2026 and today's visit is 10/17/2026. The plan is…
options: Active — the effective date has passed
Inactive — cards expire yearly
Active only for emergencies
Cannot be determined from the card
questions.explanation: A passed effective date with no termination date means the plan is active. But the card alone isn't enough — always run the 270 to confirm, since coverage can terminate mid-year.
questions.hint: Effective date passed + no end date = ?

questions.q: The 271 response shows coverage status 'INACTIVE'. What do you do?
options: Bill the visit anyway
Tell the patient and collect self-pay or reschedule
Ignore it — the card looked fine
Change the status to active in the system
questions.explanation: INACTIVE means no coverage — billing it guarantees a denial. Tell the patient upfront, offer self-pay options or reschedule. Never alter payer data to force a claim through.
questions.hint: What happens if you bill inactive coverage?

questions.q: What's the difference between the member ID and the group number?
options: They're the same thing
Member ID identifies the patient; group number identifies the employer plan
Group number is the patient's SSN
Member ID is only for dental plans
questions.explanation: The member ID is unique to the patient (like an account number). The group number identifies the employer's plan with the payer. Both go on the claim — wrong group number routes to the wrong benefits.
questions.hint: Which one is unique to the person vs the employer?

questions.q: A patient has two insurance plans. Which is primary?
options: The one with the lower copay
The patient's own employer plan (before a spouse's plan)
Whichever the patient prefers
The one that was added most recently
questions.explanation: Coordination of benefits (COB) rules: the patient's own employer coverage is primary over a spouse's plan. For children, the 'birthday rule' applies (parent whose birthday comes first in the year is primary). Billing the wrong order causes denials.
questions.hint: Whose employer plan comes first?

questions.q: The insurance card says 'Referral required for specialist'. The patient is seeing a specialist today without one. What happens?
options: The claim will pay normally
The claim will likely deny — obtain the referral first
The copay is waived
It only matters for surgeries
questions.explanation: HMO-style plans require referrals before specialist visits. Without one, the claim denies. Check referral requirements during verification — it's part of the 271 benefits, not just the card.
questions.hint: What does 'referral required' mean for payment?

title: Charge Entry & Claim Creation
description: Professional vs institutional claims, key claim fields, and charge-to-claim linking.

questions.q: A physician sees a patient in the office and also interprets the patient's X-ray at the hospital the same day. How many claims result, and on which forms?
options: One claim on the CMS-1500 covering everything
Two claims: the office visit on CMS-1500/837P (professional) and the X-ray interpretation on UB-04/837I (institutional)
One claim on the UB-04
Two claims, both on the CMS-1500
questions.explanation: The form follows the biller, not the service. The physician's professional services go on the CMS-1500 (837P electronic), while the hospital's facility services go on the UB-04 (837I). One visit can legitimately produce two claims from two billers.
questions.hint: Ask who is billing — the doctor or the facility?

questions.q: Which set of fields is required and high-impact when creating a claim?
options: The patient's preferred pharmacy and emergency contact hobbies
Correct patient demographics, NPI, diagnosis codes with pointers, procedure codes, dates of service, and charges
Only the total dollar amount
The physician's personal mobile number
questions.explanation: Claims are adjudicated by machines first. Missing or wrong demographics, NPI, diagnosis pointers, CPT codes, dates of service, or charges cause rejections or denials. Every one of these fields must be accurate.
questions.hint: Think about what a payer's computer needs to decide payment.

questions.q: What does 'charge-to-claim linking' mean in practice?
options: Connecting each entered charge (CPT + ICD + amount + date) to the correct claim so nothing is unbilled or double-billed
Linking the patient's chart to their email address
Connecting the clearinghouse directly to the bank
Merging two different patients' records
questions.explanation: Every charge entered must land on exactly one claim. Poor linking causes lost revenue (charges never billed) or compliance risk (charges billed twice). Charge entry and claim creation must reconcile with each other.
questions.hint: One charge, one claim — no orphans, no duplicates.

questions.q: A charge is entered for CPT 99214 with a date of service after the patient's discharge date. What is the most likely outcome?
options: It will be paid normally
It will be rejected or denied — the date of service does not make sense
The payer will double the payment as a courtesy
Nothing — dates of service do not matter
questions.explanation: Dates of service must be logical and fall within the encounter. A service dated after discharge (or before admission) fails basic validity checks at the clearinghouse or payer and will be rejected.
questions.hint: Would a payer believe a visit happened after the patient left?

questions.q: Why is it risky to copy last month's charge entry as a template for this month's visit?
options: There is no risk — it is faster and always accurate
The diagnosis, procedures, and payer rules may have changed — copying creates coding errors and denials
Using templates is illegal in all states
The system deletes templates automatically each month
questions.explanation: Each encounter is unique. Copying charges forward (cloning) carries over codes that may not match today's documentation, producing mismatches, medical-necessity denials, and potential upcoding exposure. Enter charges from today's documentation.
questions.hint: Same patient, different day, different story.

title: Medical Coding Basics
description: Learn ICD-10-CM, CPT, and HCPCS-II roles, diagnosis pointers, and mismatch denials.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the three coding systems?
options: ICD-10-CM codes what was done; CPT codes why it was done
ICD-10-CM codes why (diagnosis), CPT codes what was done (procedure), HCPCS-II codes supplies and drugs
All three code the same thing and are interchangeable
HCPCS-II codes diagnoses; ICD-10-CM codes procedures
questions.explanation: ICD-10-CM captures the diagnosis (the reason for care), CPT captures the procedure or service performed, and HCPCS Level II covers supplies, DME, and drugs. They work together on a claim and none replaces another.
questions.hint: Match each system to 'why,' 'what,' or 'with what.'

questions.q: A patient is seen for chest pain. Which ICD-10-CM code fits?
options: I20.9 (chest pain, unspecified)
S82.41XA (fracture, initial encounter)
C50.111 (malignant neoplasm of breast)
Z00.00 (general exam without abnormal findings)
questions.explanation: I20.9 is the unspecified chest-pain code. The fracture and neoplasm codes describe entirely different conditions, and Z00.00 is for a routine exam — using it for a symptomatic visit would misrepresent the encounter.
questions.hint: Pick the code that names the symptom the patient reported.

questions.q: The visit is a moderate-complexity established-patient office visit. Which CPT code is most likely?
options: 90837 (60-minute psychotherapy)
A4232 (syringe supply code)
99281 (low-level emergency department visit)
questions.explanation: 99213 is the standard code for a moderate established-patient office visit. 90837 is a timed psychotherapy code, A4232 is a supply code, and 99281 belongs to the emergency department — the setting and service must match the code.
questions.hint: Office visit, established patient, moderate complexity.

questions.q: What is a diagnosis pointer, and why does it matter?
options: A note from the doctor about follow-up steps
The link on the claim connecting each procedure (CPT) to the diagnosis (ICD-10-CM) that justifies it
A modifier that increases the payment amount
The patient's signature authorizing the claim
questions.explanation: Diagnosis pointers tell the payer which diagnosis supports each billed service. Without a valid pointer linking a covered diagnosis to the procedure, the payer cannot establish medical necessity and will deny the line.
questions.hint: It 'points' from the procedure to its reason.

questions.q: A claim denies with CO-50 (medical necessity). The CPT was for a knee MRI, but the linked ICD-10-CM was for a routine physical. What went wrong?
options: The codes do not support each other — the diagnosis does not justify the procedure
The claim was filed too late
The payer's system was down that day
The patient's copay was not collected
questions.explanation: CO-50 means the payer found no medical necessity: a routine-physical diagnosis does not justify a knee MRI. The fix is accurate coding that reflects the true clinical reason — never changing codes just to chase payment.
questions.hint: Read the denial literally: not medically necessary.

title: Claim Creation
description: Build a professional CMS-1500 claim from a completed charge — the bridge from clinical to billing.

questions.q: What is the CMS-1500 form used for?
options: Hospital inpatient billing
Professional (physician/supplier) claims
Dental claims only
Pharmacy prescriptions
questions.explanation: The CMS-1500 (837P electronic) is for professional claims — physician offices, clinics, suppliers. Hospitals use the UB-04 (837I). Using the wrong form guarantees rejection.
questions.hint: 1500 = professional, UB-04 = institutional

questions.q: A charge must be in what status before you can create a claim from it?
options: Any status works
READY — completed and unlinked
Already linked to another claim
Deleted
questions.explanation: Only READY charges (completed, not yet claimed) can become claims. Creating two claims from one charge is duplicate billing — a compliance violation.
questions.hint: Can one charge become two claims?

questions.q: Which diagnosis pointer links the procedure to the diagnosis on the claim?
options: The patient's phone number
The diagnosis pointer (1, 2, 3, 4) on each service line
The claim number
The provider's NPI
questions.explanation: Each service line carries diagnosis pointers referencing the diagnosis codes (1-4). This tells the payer WHY each procedure was done — wrong pointers cause medical-necessity denials.
questions.hint: How does the payer know which diagnosis justifies which procedure?

questions.q: The charge has CPT 99213 and ICD E11.9. When creating the claim, you should…
options: Change the codes to get paid more
Carry the codes exactly as documented
Leave the diagnosis blank
Add extra procedures for revenue
questions.explanation: The claim must mirror the documented charge exactly. Changing codes to increase payment is upcoding (fraud). Adding undocumented procedures is also fraud. The claim is a billing translation, not a rewrite.
questions.hint: What happens if you change codes for money?

questions.q: After creating a claim, what status should it have before submission?
options: PAID
DRAFT — validated but not yet sent
DENIED
Written off
questions.explanation: New claims start as DRAFT. They must pass scrubber validation, THEN be submitted. Skipping validation is how dirty claims reach the payer and deny.
questions.hint: What comes between creation and submission?

title: Claim Validation
description: Run the 13-rule scrubber, fix flags, and validate claims before submission.

questions.q: What does a clearinghouse do during claim scrubbing?
options: Deletes old claims from the system
Checks the 837 claim file for errors (missing fields, invalid codes, format issues), translates it, and forwards it to the payer
Pays the provider directly
Decides the allowed amount for each service
questions.explanation: The clearinghouse scrubs the electronic 837 claim for format and data errors, translates it into the payer's required format, and forwards it. It does not set payment amounts — that is the payer's adjudication step.
questions.hint: 'Scrub' means clean the claim before the payer sees it.

questions.q: A claim comes back as 'rejected.' How is that different from 'denied'?
options: They are the same thing
Rejected means the claim never entered the payer's system (bad data or format), usually caught by the clearinghouse; denied means the payer processed it and refused payment
Rejected is always worse than denied
Denied claims can never be fixed or resubmitted
questions.explanation: This is the classic trainee confusion. A rejection means the claim bounced before adjudication — fix the data and resubmit. A denial means the payer adjudicated it and said no — it needs a correction, an appeal, or a write-off. The workflows are completely different.
questions.hint: Rejection happens before the payer decides; denial IS the payer's decision.

questions.q: What are NCCI edits?
options: A type of insurance identification card
National Correct Coding Initiative rules that block improper code combinations (unbundling) on a claim
A method for paying providers electronically
A patient satisfaction survey
questions.explanation: NCCI edits are CMS rules that prevent providers from billing separately for services that should be bundled together (unbundling). Scrubbers check claims against these edits before submission.
questions.hint: 'Correct Coding' is in the name — they enforce coding correctness.

questions.q: A commercial payer requires claims within 90 days of service. A claim is submitted on day 120. What happens?
options: It will be paid with a small late penalty
It will be denied for timely filing (CO-29), and the provider usually cannot bill the patient
The payer extends the deadline automatically
The balance is transferred to the patient as a courtesy bill
questions.explanation: CO-29 timely-filing denials are generally final: the deadline passed and the loss falls on the provider, not the patient. Medicare allows about 12 months; commercial plans are often 90 to 180 days. Calendar control is an RCM essential.
questions.hint: Deadlines in billing are hard walls, not suggestions.

questions.q: Before submitting, the scrubber flags 'missing diagnosis pointer on line 2.' What should the biller do?
options: Submit anyway — the payer will figure it out
Fix the pointer so line 2 links to a valid diagnosis, then resubmit
Delete line 2 to make the error go away
Change the diagnosis to one the payer prefers
questions.explanation: A missing diagnosis pointer means the payer cannot establish medical necessity for that line, so it will deny. The correct action is to link the proper diagnosis from the documentation. Deleting the line loses revenue; changing the diagnosis to please the payer is falsification.
questions.hint: Fix the data — don't hide it and don't fake it.

title: Claim Submission
description: Scrub, validate, and transmit the 837P to the payer — then read the adjudication result.

questions.q: What does the claim scrubber check before submission?
options: The provider's lunch schedule
13+ rules: demographics, codes, medical necessity, duplicates, timely filing
Only the claim total
The patient's credit score
questions.explanation: The scrubber runs the same edits the payer will — demographics match, valid CPT/ICD, diagnosis pointers, NPI, place of service, duplicates, timely filing. Catching errors here prevents denials.
questions.hint: What would the payer check?

questions.q: The scrubber flags an error. You should…
options: Submit anyway and hope
Fix the error, re-validate, then submit
Delete the claim
Submit to a different payer
questions.explanation: Fix → re-validate → submit. Submitting a flagged claim guarantees a denial or rejection. The scrubber exists to catch what humans miss.
questions.hint: What's the point of the scrubber?

questions.q: What is the 837P transaction?
options: The paper claim form
The electronic professional claim sent to the payer
The payment from the payer
The eligibility check
questions.explanation: 837P = electronic professional claim (the digital CMS-1500). 837I is institutional. 835 is the remittance/payment, 270/271 is eligibility.

questions.q: After submission, the payer returns 'PAID'. What does this mean?
options: The full billed amount was paid
The claim adjudicated — check allowed, paid, adjustment, and patient responsibility
No further action is ever needed
The patient owes nothing
questions.explanation: PAID means adjudicated, not 'paid in full'. Always reconcile: allowed amount, payer paid, contractual adjustment, and patient responsibility. There may still be a patient balance to collect.
questions.hint: Does PAID mean the whole billed amount?

questions.q: After submission, the payer returns 'DENIED' with CO-16. What's the first step?
options: Write it off immediately
Read the denial reason, fix the missing/invalid information, and rebill
Sue the payer
Bill the patient the full amount
questions.explanation: CO-16 = missing/invalid information. Read what exactly is missing, correct it, and rebill. Most CO-16 denials are fixable — writing off without trying loses revenue.
questions.hint: What does CO-16 tell you?

title: Payment Posting
description: ERA vs EOB, allowed amounts, contractual adjustments, and underpayment detection.

questions.q: Worked example: CPT 90837 billed $200, allowed $140. What is the contractual adjustment, and why?
options: $60 — the difference between billed and allowed, written off per the payer contract (CO-45)
$28 — the patient's coinsurance amount
$112 — the payer's payment amount
$200 — the full billed amount is written off
questions.explanation: The contractual adjustment is billed minus allowed: $200 minus $140 = $60, coded CO-45. The provider agreed to this rate in the payer contract, so it can never be billed to the patient. The $28 is patient coinsurance and the $112 is the payer's check.
questions.hint: The contract says 'we pay $140 for this code' — the rest is the adjustment.

questions.q: Same example (billed $200, allowed $140, coinsurance $28). How much does the payer actually pay, and what is patient responsibility?
options: Payer pays $140; patient owes $0
Payer pays $112; patient owes $28 coinsurance
Payer pays $200; patient owes $28
Payer pays $60; patient owes $140
questions.explanation: The allowed $140 splits into patient coinsurance ($28, PR-2) and the payer's share ($140 minus $28 = $112). The payer never pays the full billed amount under a contract, and the write-off is never the patient's bill. Check: $60 + $28 + $112 = $200.
questions.hint: Allowed equals payer share plus patient share: $140 = $112 + $28.

questions.q: What is the difference between an ERA and an EOB?
options: They are identical documents
The ERA (835) is the electronic remittance file used for posting payments; the EOB is the patient-facing explanation of benefits, not used for posting
The EOB is electronic and the ERA is paper
The ERA is sent to the patient and the EOB to the provider
questions.explanation: The ERA (835 transaction) is the machine-readable file the billing system auto-posts from. The EOB is the human-readable statement, often sent to the patient. Posting from an EOB by hand is slow and error-prone; the ERA is the posting source of truth.
questions.hint: 'Electronic' is in the name — which one would a computer read?

questions.q: A claim shows $0 payment but no denial code. What is the most likely explanation?
options: It must be a denial
Zero pay does not always mean denial — the payment may have applied entirely to the deductible, or the remit has not fully processed
The payer lost the claim
The patient already paid everything
questions.explanation: Zero pay does not equal denial — this is a core poster skill. If the allowed amount went entirely to the patient's unmet deductible, the payer correctly pays $0 and the balance is patient responsibility. Always read the remark codes before assuming a denial.
questions.hint: Who pays first when a deductible is unmet? The patient — so the payer's check can be $0.

questions.q: The payer's remit shows an allowed amount LOWER than the contracted rate for that CPT. What should the poster do?
options: Accept it and move on
Flag it as a potential underpayment and route it for contract-based follow-up
Bill the patient for the difference
Delete the payment and repost it at the higher amount
questions.explanation: Underpayment detection is a core payment-posting skill: compare the allowed amount against the contracted fee schedule. If the payer shorted the contracted rate, that is the payer's error to pursue — never shift it to the patient or falsify the posting.
questions.hint: The contract is the referee — check the payer's number against it.

title: A/R Follow-up & KPIs
description: Aging buckets, days in A/R, benchmark KPIs, and claim prioritization.

questions.q: Claims sit in aging buckets: 0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 91+ days. A claim is 75 days old with no payer response. What does that tell you?
options: It is fine — payers routinely take 75 days
It sits in the 61-90 bucket and needs active follow-up now, before it slides into 91+ where collectability drops
It should be written off immediately
Aging buckets are only for management reports
questions.explanation: Aging buckets prioritize work because older balances are harder and less likely to collect. A 75-day claim with no response is stuck and needs a status call or appeal now. Waiting turns a follow-up task into a write-off.
questions.hint: Money gets colder with age — work the warmest old claims first.

questions.q: How is 'days in A/R' calculated?
options: Total accounts receivable divided by average daily charges
Total charges divided by the number of patients
Denied claims divided by total claims
Cash collected divided by days in the month
questions.explanation: Days in A/R equals total accounts receivable divided by average daily charges. It answers: how many days of revenue are sitting uncollected? Lower is better — best-in-class is under 40 days, with top performers under 35.
questions.hint: It is a 'how long until we are paid' number.

questions.q: Your practice shows: clean claim rate 88%, denial rate 9%, days in A/R 55. Benchmarks are >95-98% clean, <5% denials, <40 days in A/R. What is the right read?
options: Everything is performing fine
All three miss benchmark — revenue leaks at submission (low clean rate), adjudication (high denials), and collection (slow A/R); fix upstream first
Only the denial rate matters
Benchmarks do not apply to smaller practices
questions.explanation: The three KPIs tell one story: claims go out dirty (88% clean), get denied (9%), and sit unpaid (55 days). Because most denials originate upstream, the highest-leverage fix is front-end quality — registration, eligibility, coding — which lifts all three numbers together.
questions.hint: Three red lights, one engine — start where claims are born.

questions.q: You have one hour for A/R follow-up. Which claims do you work first?
options: The newest claims in the 0-30 bucket
High-dollar claims in the 61-90 and 91+ buckets that are closest to timely-filing or appeal deadlines
Claims in alphabetical order by patient name
Only the smallest balances, to clear volume
questions.explanation: Prioritization equals dollars at risk times time sensitivity. High-value aging claims near filing or appeal deadlines lose everything if they expire; new claims still have time. Work the intersection of big money and expiring soon.
questions.hint: Save what is about to be lost forever first.

questions.q: What is net collection rate, and why does it matter more than gross collection rate?
options: They measure exactly the same thing

Net collection rate is collections divided by charges minus contractual adjustments; it measures how much of what you are actually allowed to collect you really collect (benchmark above 95-96%). The gross rate is distorted by write-offs
Net collection rate is always 100%
It measures patient satisfaction scores
questions.explanation: Gross collections can look fine even while contractual adjustments hide underperformance. Net collection rate strips out the contracted write-offs and asks: of every collectible dollar, how many did we get? Above 95 to 96% is the benchmark.
questions.hint: Judge yourself on dollars you were allowed to keep, not dollars you billed.

title: Denial Management
description: Group codes, CARCs, bundling, corrected claims vs appeals, and the denial workflow.

questions.q: A denial carries group code CO. A second carries PR. What is the practical difference?
options: There is no practical difference
CO (Contractual Obligation) means the provider absorbs it and cannot bill the patient; PR (Patient Responsibility) means it can be billed to the patient
CO means the patient pays; PR means the provider pays
CO denials are always appealable; PR denials never are
questions.explanation: Group codes decide who owns the balance. CO means the provider is contractually obligated to absorb it — billing the patient would violate the payer contract. PR means the balance legitimately belongs to the patient (deductible, coinsurance, or properly-noticed non-covered services).
questions.hint: C is contractual (the provider's problem); P is the patient's.

questions.q: Two denials arrive: one CO-96, one PR-96. What is the difference, and when is PR-96 appropriate?
options: They are identical denials

CO-96 is a non-covered charge absorbed by the provider; PR-96 is a non-covered charge billable to the patient, typically when the patient signed advance notice (ABN) or a GY modifier shows the service is statutorily excluded
PR-96 means the provider must absorb the charge
CO-96 is always a payer mistake
questions.explanation: Both are 'non-covered,' but the group code changes everything. PR-96 is only valid when the patient was properly notified in advance (for example an ABN) or the service is statutorily excluded (GY modifier). Without that, it stays CO-96 and the provider absorbs it.
questions.hint: Same CARC, different owner — what paperwork lets you bill the patient?

questions.q: A claim denies CO-97 (bundling). The biller used modifier -59. The NCCI modifier indicator for this edit is '1'. What is the best next step?
options: Resubmit with -59 again and hope it passes
Check whether a more specific modifier (XE, XS, XP, or XU) accurately describes distinct services, and only rebill if documentation supports it; otherwise accept the bundling
Bill the patient for the bundled service
Delete the second procedure line from the claim
questions.explanation: CO-97 means the payer bundled the services per NCCI. Modifier -59 is the vague 'distinct service' flag; payers prefer the specific X{EPSU} modifiers — but only when documentation truly supports distinct services. Appending modifiers to force payment is upcoding risk.
questions.hint: Specific beats vague — but the documentation must earn the modifier.

questions.q: A denial needs fixing. When do you send a corrected claim (frequency 7) versus filing a formal appeal?
options: They are the same process

A corrected claim (bill type frequency 7) fixes data or coding errors and replaces the claim; an appeal disputes the payer's decision with documentation and is used when the claim was correct but the payer's judgment is challenged
Always file an appeal first
Corrected claims are only used for Medicare
questions.explanation: Frequency 7 replaces a claim that had fixable errors (wrong code, missing modifier). An appeal argues the payer decided wrongly on a correct claim and needs medical records plus a letter. Choosing wrong wastes weeks: appealing a data error, or 'correcting' a judgment call.
questions.hint: Fix your mistake with a corrected claim; fight their mistake with an appeal.

questions.q: A denial letter arrives 60 days after the remit date. The payer's appeal window is 90 days from the remit date. What must happen?
options: Nothing — there is still plenty of time
The appeal must be filed within the 90-day window (30 days remain) — track deadlines per payer, because missing them forfeits the money
Appeal windows reset whenever you call the payer
Appeal windows only apply to Medicare
questions.explanation: Appeal windows (typically 30 to 90 days, payer-specific) are hard deadlines measured from the remit date, not from when you noticed the denial. Strong teams overturn most well-built appeals — but only when filed on time. Calendar every denial.
questions.hint: The clock started at the remit, not at your desk.

questions.q: What is the correct denial-management workflow?
options: Write off every denial immediately to keep A/R clean
Classify the denial (code and group), gather documentation, correct or appeal, track the outcome, then fix the root cause upstream so it stops recurring
Resubmit the identical claim every week until it pays
Call the payer and argue until they reverse it
questions.explanation: Denial management is a loop, not a single action: classify to learn the real reason, resolve the individual claim correctly, then fix the upstream cause (registration, coding, authorization) so the whole denial class shrinks. Writing everything off or blindly resubmitting burns money.
questions.hint: Treat the disease (root cause), not just the symptom (one claim).

title: Full-Cycle Clean Claim Challenge
description: Follow fictional patient Sarah Johnson from registration through payment and A/R — including a denial twist.

questions.q: Stage 1 — Registration: at check-in, the front desk copies Sarah Johnson's insurance card but does not verify eligibility. What is the risk?
options: No risk — the insurance card is sufficient proof
The card may be expired or the plan may have changed; without a 270/271 check, the visit may be uninsured and the claim denied
Verification is only needed for surgeries
The payer verifies eligibility automatically on claim receipt
questions.explanation: A card is a snapshot, not proof — coverage can lapse or change between visits. The 271 response confirms active-on-date-of-service, benefits, and authorization flags. Skipping eligibility verification is the number one beginner mistake and a top source of denials.
questions.hint: Cards expire; eligibility is checked live.

questions.q: Stage 2 — Coding: Sarah is seen for right ankle pain after a fall. The coder links CPT 99213 to ICD-10-CM S82.41XA (fracture of right lower leg, initial encounter). Is this sound?
options: Yes — the diagnosis supports the visit, and the 7th character 'A' correctly marks an initial encounter
No — ankle pain can never be coded
Yes, but the 7th character does not matter
No — fractures can never be initial encounters
questions.explanation: The fracture diagnosis justifies the office visit, and the 'A' seventh character correctly marks an initial encounter. Accurate, specific coding with valid diagnosis pointers is what survives medical-necessity review.
questions.hint: Does the 'why' support the 'what'? Yes.

questions.q: Stage 3 — Claim: the claim goes out on a CMS-1500 (837P). Why is that the right form?
options: It is the only claim form that exists
The physician's professional services are billed by the provider on the professional claim form — the form follows the biller
The UB-04 is the form used by physicians
Claim forms do not matter as long as the amounts are right
questions.explanation: The physician's professional services belong on the CMS-1500/837P. If a hospital facility were billing for the same encounter's facility costs, that would go on the UB-04/837I. The form follows the biller, not the service.
questions.hint: Who is billing — the physician or the facility?

questions.q: Stage 4 — Denial twist: the payer denies one line with CO-97 (bundling). The two procedures were a single ankle X-ray interpretation bundled into the visit per NCCI, with modifier indicator '0'. What is the right move?
options: Append modifier -59 and rebill to force payment
Accept the bundling — indicator '0' means no modifier can override the edit, and the documentation does not support separate payment
Bill Sarah Johnson for the X-ray interpretation
Resubmit the identical claim every week
questions.explanation: An NCCI indicator of '0' means the edit cannot be bypassed with any modifier. Forcing payment with -59 would be improper. The payer applied the rule correctly, so the right move is to accept the bundling rather than fight a correct edit.
questions.hint: Indicator 0 means the edit always wins.

questions.q: Stage 5 — Payment & A/R: the remit arrives — billed $180, allowed $150, CO-45 $30 write-off, patient coinsurance PR-2 $30, payer pays $120. Sarah's $30 balance sits in A/R at 35 days with no payment. What is the right action?
options: Write off the $30 immediately
Verify the math ($30 + $30 + $120 = $180), confirm the balance is truly patient responsibility, then send the patient statement and follow up — it is in the 31-60 bucket
Resubmit the claim to the payer
Dispute that the balance exists
questions.explanation: First verify posting accuracy: $180 equals the $30 write-off plus $30 patient share plus $120 payer payment. The $30 is legitimate patient responsibility (PR-2), not a payer error, so the claim does not go back to the payer — it goes to patient collections with statements and follow-up in the 31-60 bucket.
questions.hint: PR on the remit means the next stop is the patient, not the payer.

title: ED Chest Pain — Documentation Gap Detection
description: Read a 5-document ED chart packet. The CT was read, but did the ED note support the exam level? Spot documentation gaps that cost revenue.

documents.content:
TRIAGE NOTE — 03/14/2026 08:42
45-year-old male presents with chest pain x 2 hours.
Pain: substernal, pressure-like, 7/10, radiates to left arm.
Associated: mild diaphoresis, no SOB.
Vitals: BP 150/95, HR 102, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 98.6F
PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia. NKDA.
ESI: 2 — placed in monitored bed, ECG ordered stat.

ED PROVIDER NOTE — 03/14/2026 09:15 — Dr. R. Patel
CHIEF COMPLAINT: Chest pain.
HPI: 45yo M with HTN/hyperlipidemia, acute substernal chest pressure x2hrs, 7/10, radiating to L arm, with diaphoresis. No SOB, no syncope. Similar episode 6 months ago — negative workup at that time.
EXAM: Brief exam performed. Patient alert, in no acute distress. Heart regular rhythm. Lungs clear.
MDM: ECG shows NSR, no ST changes. Troponin pending. CT chest ordered to rule out PE given tachycardia. Will observe.
PLAN: Serial troponins, cardiology consult if positive. Disposition pending results.

CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST — 03/14/2026 10:03
INDICATION: Chest pain, tachycardia — rule out pulmonary embolism.
TECHNIQUE: Axial images with IV contrast.
FINDINGS: No filling defect in pulmonary arteries. No PE identified. Lungs clear, no infiltrate. No pleural effusion. Cardiac silhouette normal.
IMPRESSION: Negative CT chest — no evidence of pulmonary embolism.
Electronically signed: Dr. S. Morrison, Radiology — 10:47

LABORATORY — 03/14/2026
Troponin I (08:55): 0.02 ng/mL [ref <0.04] — NORMAL
Troponin I (11:55): 0.03 ng/mL [ref <0.04] — NORMAL
CBC: WBC 7.2, Hgb 14.1, Plt 245 — all normal
BMP: Na 140, K 4.1, Cr 0.9, Glu 102 — normal
Lipid panel: Total 228 (H), LDL 148 (H)
ECG (09:00): Normal sinus rhythm, no ST elevation/depression, no T-wave abnormality.

ED DISCHARGE SUMMARY — 03/14/2026 13:20
DIAGNOSES: Chest pain, unspecified (R07.89); Hypertension (I10); Hyperlipidemia (E78.5)
COURSE: Serial troponins negative x2, ECG non-ischemic, CT negative for PE. Cardiology not consulted — low suspicion for ACS after negative workup.
DISPOSITION: Discharged home in stable condition.
INSTRUCTIONS: Return for worsening pain, SOB, syncope. Follow up with PCP in 3-5 days. Aspirin 81mg daily started.

questions.q: Based on the ED Provider Note tab, what level of exam was documented?
options: Comprehensive exam
Detailed exam
Brief/problem-focused exam
No exam documented
questions.explanation: The note literally states 'Brief exam performed' with only 2-3 systems noted. This supports only a problem-focused exam level — a documentation gap, since the MDM was moderate-to-high complexity (CT ordered, PE workup, serial troponins).
questions.hint: Read the EXAM section of the ED Provider Note carefully.

questions.q: The CT chest was ordered and read (see CT Chest Report tab). What is the coding/documentation concern here?
options: CT was not medically necessary
The ED note's exam level doesn't support the MDM complexity — revenue is left on the table
CT reports can't be billed from the ED
There is no concern
questions.explanation: The MDM involved independent interpretation discussions, PE workup, and serial testing — but the exam was documented as 'brief.' Better exam documentation would support a higher E/M level (99284/99285 vs 99283). This is the classic documentation gap.
questions.hint: Compare the EXAM section against the MDM/PLAN complexity.

questions.q: Based on the Discharge Summary tab, what is the correct primary diagnosis code?
options: I10 (Hypertension)
E78.5 (Hyperlipidemia)
R07.89 (Chest pain, unspecified)
I25.10 (Coronary artery disease)
questions.explanation: R07.89 is listed first — the chest pain was the reason for the encounter. Never code suspected/rule-out conditions (like ACS or PE) as if they were confirmed; the workup was negative.
questions.hint: Which diagnosis was the reason for the visit?

questions.q: The troponins were negative x2 and the CT was negative for PE. How should the 'rule-out PE' and 'rule-out MI' be coded?
options: Code I26.99 (PE) and I21.9 (MI) since they were considered
Code only confirmed diagnoses — R07.89, I10, E78.5
Code Z03.89 (observation for suspected condition)
Code R07.89 plus I26.99 as secondary
questions.explanation: Rule-out, suspected, and probable conditions are NOT coded in the ED/outpatient setting. Code only what is confirmed: chest pain (R07.89), HTN, hyperlipidemia.
questions.hint: Were PE or MI confirmed by the workup?

questions.q: What is the single most valuable documentation improvement the provider could make for this encounter?
options: Add more HPI elements
Document a detailed exam matching the MDM complexity
Order more tests
Add a longer discharge summary
questions.explanation: The MDM clearly supports moderate-high complexity (independent test interpretation, PE workup, serial troponins). A detailed exam would support 99284 instead of 99283 — roughly $100+ in additional legitimate revenue per visit.
questions.hint: Where is the mismatch between work done and work documented?

title: Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy — Op Report Coding
description: Code from a real-style operative report. Intraoperative cholangiogram was performed — does that change the CPT? Avoid the classic 47562/47600 trap.

documents.content:
HISTORY & PHYSICAL — 03/10/2026 — Dr. L. Chen
38-year-old female with 3-month history of episodic RUQ pain after fatty meals, radiating to right shoulder. Ultrasound 03/05: cholelithiasis, gallbladder wall 4mm, no CBD dilation, no pericholecystic fluid.
PMH: None. PSH: None. Allergies: PCN (rash).
ASSESSMENT: Symptomatic cholelithiasis.
PLAN: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy, possible intraoperative cholangiogram.

OPERATIVE REPORT — 03/12/2026 — Dr. L. Chen, Surgeon
PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Symptomatic cholelithiasis.
POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Cholelithiasis with chronic cholecystitis.
PROCEDURE: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy with intraoperative cholangiogram.
ANESTHESIA: General endotracheal.
FINDINGS: Gallbladder moderately inflamed with adhesions to omentum. Cystic duct and artery identified. No CBD stones on cholangiogram.
DESCRIPTION: Four-port laparoscopic technique. Pneumoperitoneum established. Adhesiolysis performed. Critical view of safety obtained. Cystic duct cannulated; intraoperative cholangiogram performed — contrast flowed freely into duodenum, no filling defects. Cystic duct and artery clipped and divided. Gallbladder dissected from liver bed and removed via umbilical port. Hemostasis achieved. Ports closed.
SPECIMEN: Gallbladder to pathology.
COMPLICATIONS: None. EBL: 25 mL.

SURGICAL PATHOLOGY — 03/14/2026
SPECIMEN: Gallbladder.
GROSS: Gallbladder 8.5 cm, wall thickened to 4mm, multiple black calculi 3-8mm.
MICROSCOPIC: Chronic cholecystitis with cholelithiasis. No dysplasia or malignancy.
DIAGNOSIS: Chronic cholecystitis with cholelithiasis (K81.1, K80.20).

ANESTHESIA RECORD — 03/12/2026
Type: General endotracheal anesthesia. ASA II.
Induction: Propofol, fentanyl, rocuronium. Maintenance: Sevoflurane.
Duration: 95 minutes. No complications.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY — 03/13/2026
PROCEDURE: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy with IOC.
COURSE: Tolerated procedure well. Diet advanced. Pain controlled.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES: Chronic cholecystitis with cholelithiasis (K81.1).
DISPOSITION: Home, POD 1. Follow up in 2 weeks.

questions.q: Based on the Operative Report tab, what is the correct CPT for the cholecystectomy?
options: 47562 (lap chole without cholangiography)
47563 (lap chole with cholangiography)
47600 (open cholecystectomy)
47610 (open cholecystectomy with cholangiography)
questions.explanation: 47563 — laparoscopic cholecystectomy WITH cholangiography. The op report explicitly states intraoperative cholangiogram was performed with contrast flowing to duodenum. 47600/47610 are OPEN procedures — wrong approach.
questions.hint: Was the procedure laparoscopic or open? Was cholangiography performed?

questions.q: Can the intraoperative cholangiogram be coded separately in addition to 47563?
options: Yes, add 74300
Yes, add 47563-59
No — cholangiography is bundled into 47563
Yes, with modifier -51
questions.explanation: No. CPT 47563 by definition includes the cholangiography. Coding it separately would be unbundling.
questions.hint: Read the CPT descriptor for 47563 carefully.

questions.q: Based on the Pathology Report tab, what ICD-10-CM codes are supported?
options: K80.20 only
K81.1 (chronic cholecystitis) + K80.20 (calculus of gallbladder)
K81.0 (acute cholecystitis)
K82.8 (other gallbladder disease)
questions.explanation: Pathology confirms chronic cholecystitis (K81.1) with cholelithiasis/calculi (K80.20). The H&P showed no acute findings — don't code acute cholecystitis.
questions.hint: What did pathology actually find — acute or chronic?

questions.q: The surgeon performed adhesiolysis to mobilize the gallbladder. Can this be coded separately?
options: Yes, add 44180
Yes, with modifier -59
No — adhesiolysis to access the surgical site is bundled
Yes, add 44005
questions.explanation: Lysis of adhesions performed to gain access to the operative site is inherent to the primary procedure and not separately reportable.
questions.hint: Was the adhesiolysis the purpose of surgery or just access?

questions.q: A coder submits 47600 for this case. What is the compliance risk?
options: None — codes are interchangeable
Upcoding: billing an open procedure when laparoscopic was performed = overpayment + audit risk
Downcoding: the facility loses money
Only a typo, no consequence
questions.explanation: 47600 (open) pays significantly more than 47562/47563 (laparoscopic). Billing the higher-paying open code for a laparoscopic procedure is upcoding — a False Claims Act exposure.
questions.hint: Compare the payment and approach of 47600 vs 47563.

title: Office Visit + Biopsy — Modifier 25
description: A separately identifiable E/M on the same day as a skin biopsy. When does modifier -25 apply — and when is it fraud to use it?

documents.content:
OFFICE NOTE — 03/18/2026 — Dr. A. Williams, Dermatology
CHIEF COMPLAINT: Changing mole on back; also here for 6-month skin check.
HPI: 52yo F notes a dark mole on upper back enlarging over 3 months, occasional itching. Also requests full skin exam — history of atypical nevi.
EXAM: Full skin exam performed. Upper back: 8mm asymmetric dark brown papule with irregular borders — suspicious for dysplastic nevus vs melanoma. Remainder of skin: 3 benign-appearing nevi, no other suspicious lesions.
ASSESSMENT: 1) Atypical nevus, upper back — biopsy recommended. 2) Skin check — no other concerning lesions.
PLAN: Shave biopsy of back lesion today (separate procedure note). Routine skin surveillance q6 months. Patient counseled on ABCDE warning signs.

PROCEDURE NOTE — 03/18/2026 — Dr. A. Williams
PROCEDURE: Shave biopsy, upper back lesion.
INDICATION: 8mm atypical pigmented lesion, rule out dysplasia/melanoma.
TECHNIQUE: Area prepped with chloraprep, anesthetized with 1% lidocaine. Shave biopsy performed at dermal level. Hemostasis with aluminum chloride. Petrolatum + bandage applied.
SPECIMEN: To pathology, labeled 'back lesion.'
COMPLICATIONS: None. Patient tolerated well.

DERMATOPATHOLOGY — 03/21/2026
SPECIMEN: Shave biopsy, upper back.
DIAGNOSIS: Dysplastic nevus, moderate atypia. Margins involved — recommend re-excision.
Note: No melanoma identified.

questions.q: Based on the Office Note tab, was a separately identifiable E/M performed?
options: No — the visit was only for the biopsy
Yes — full skin exam + counseling beyond the biopsy decision
No — same-day E/M is never billable with a procedure
Yes, but only if the patient is new
questions.explanation: Yes. The provider performed a full skin exam, evaluated 3 other nevi, and counseled on surveillance — work significantly beyond the biopsy decision itself. This supports 99213-25.
questions.hint: Did the provider do work beyond deciding to biopsy?

questions.q: What is the correct coding for this encounter?
options: 11100 only
99213 only
questions.explanation: 99213-25 (separately identifiable E/M) + 11100 (biopsy). Modifier -25 goes on the E/M, never on the procedure. -59 on an E/M is always wrong.
questions.hint: Which code gets the -25?

questions.q: A coder appends modifier -59 to the E/M instead of -25. Why is this wrong?
options: -59 pays less than -25
Modifier -59 is for procedures only — never on E/M codes
-59 requires a different diagnosis
It is actually correct
questions.explanation: Modifier -59 (distinct procedural service) is defined for procedure codes only. Appending it to an E/M is a coding error that will deny or trigger audit. -25 is the E/M modifier.
questions.hint: What code type does -59 belong to?

questions.q: Based on the Pathology Report tab, what diagnosis supports the biopsy (11100)?
options: D22.5 (benign nevus of trunk)
D48.5 (neoplasm of uncertain behavior of skin)
C43.59 (melanoma of trunk)
L98.9 (skin disorder, unspecified)
questions.explanation: D48.5 — neoplasm of uncertain behavior. At the time of biopsy the lesion was suspicious (atypical, rule out melanoma). Don't code melanoma (not confirmed) or benign nevus (contradicted by atypia).
questions.hint: Was melanoma confirmed? Was the lesion clearly benign?

title: Denial Workup: CO-29 Timely Filing
description: A $285 claim denied CO-29 — filed past the payer's deadline. Work the denial: compute filing days, determine if it's appealable, and choose write-off vs appeal with proof.

questions.q: ERA shows: DOS 2026-03-10, payer UHC commercial, received 2026-06-15, denied CO-29. How many days after DOS was the claim filed, and what is UHC commercial's timely-filing limit?
options: 97 days — past UHC's 90-day limit
87 days — within the 90-day limit, so CO-29 is wrong
107 days — past the limit, but UHC allows 120 days
97 days — within Medicare's 365-day limit, so this must be Medicare
questions.explanation: March 10 → June 15 = 97 days. UHC commercial timely filing is 90 days, so the claim is 7 days late — CO-29 is correct. (Medicare allows 365 days, but this is UHC commercial.)
questions.hint: Count the days March 10 → June 15, then recall UHC commercial's limit.

questions.q: The biller says 'let's just appeal it.' When is a CO-29 denial actually appealable?
options: Always — every denial can be appealed
Only with proof of timely filing (e.g., clearinghouse acceptance report showing the original was filed on time)
Only if the billed amount is over $500
Never — CO-29 is final
questions.explanation: CO-29 overturns only with proof the claim WAS filed on time — a clearinghouse 999 acceptance, EDI transmission log, or certified-mail receipt. An appeal with no new proof is auto-denied. Without proof, policy is usually write-off.
questions.hint: What new fact could change the payer's mind about the filing date?

questions.q: You find the clearinghouse acceptance report: the claim was first transmitted on 2026-06-02 (84 days after DOS). What is the correct next step?
options: Write off — 84 days is still past the limit
Appeal with the acceptance report attached as proof of timely filing
Rebill as a new claim with today's date
Bill the patient the full $285
questions.explanation: 84 days is WITHIN the 90-day limit — the denial was wrong. Appeal with the clearinghouse acceptance report as proof of timely filing. Never rebill as new (that's a duplicate) and never bill the patient for a payer filing error.
questions.hint: 84 < 90. The denial is wrong — what fixes it?

questions.q: No proof of timely filing exists — the claim truly went out late. What should happen to the $285 balance?
options: Bill the patient — it's their insurance
Write off as a timely-filing adjustment; feed the root cause upstream
Keep rebilling every 30 days until it pays
Appeal anyway — payers sometimes pay late claims
questions.explanation: Late filing is the provider's fault — the patient cannot be billed for it (and most contracts prohibit it). Write off the balance and fix the root cause: why did this claim sit 97 days? Diary/alert workflows prevent repeats.
questions.hint: Whose fault is a late filing? Can that party bill the patient?

questions.q: Which workflow prevents CO-29 denials from happening in the first place?
options: Appealing every denial within 30 days
Aging-based work queues with alerts at 14/30 days and payer-specific filing calendars
Billing patients faster
Using more modifiers
questions.explanation: Prevention beats appeals: work A/R by age, set diary alerts well before each payer's deadline (UHC 90d, Aetna 120d, Medicare 365d), and escalate stuck claims early. CO-29 is almost always a workflow failure, not a payer error.
questions.hint: CO-29 is a calendar problem — what calendar discipline fixes it?

title: Denial Workup: CO-16 + N286 Missing Referring NPI
description: A $1,450 MRI denied CO-16 with remark N286 — the referring provider identifier is missing. Read the RARC, find the gap, and correct it. (Hint: never appeal this.)

questions.q: ERA line: 70553 (MRI brain with contrast), billed $1,450, paid $0, CO-16 + N286. What does N286 tell you?
options: The claim was filed too late
The referring provider's NPI is missing or invalid
The service is bundled into another procedure
The patient has other insurance
questions.explanation: N286 = missing/invalid referring provider identifier. CO-16 is the generic 'claim lacks information' bucket; the RARC pinpoints exactly what's missing. For advanced imaging, the ordering/referring NPI is required.
questions.hint: N286 is about WHO ordered it.

questions.q: The correct fix for CO-16 + N286 is:
options: Appeal with a letter of medical necessity
Submit a corrected claim with the referring provider's valid 10-digit NPI
Write off — imaging without a referral is never payable
Bill the patient $1,450
questions.explanation: CO-16 is a 'fix and resubmit' denial, never an appeal — an appeal argues the payer was wrong, but here the claim was genuinely incomplete. Add the referring NPI (10 digits, active) and send a corrected claim.
questions.hint: CO-16 means the claim itself was broken. Appeals don't fix broken claims.

questions.q: You look up the referring physician: NPI 123456789 (9 digits). The claim still denies. Why?
options: The payer doesn't cover MRIs
NPIs are always exactly 10 digits — this one is invalid
The referring physician must be in-network
CO-16 always requires an appeal
questions.explanation: NPI is always 10 digits — 9 digits fails validation (the scrubber rule NPI-001 catches this pre-submission). Get the correct 10-digit NPI from NPPES and resubmit.
questions.hint: Count the digits. What does the scrubber require?

questions.q: After adding the valid referring NPI, the corrected claim pays in full. What should the biller document to prevent repeats?
options: Nothing — denials happen
Flag the ordering workflow: advanced imaging orders must capture the referring NPI at scheduling
Always appeal CO-16 first
Stop ordering MRIs
questions.explanation: Root-cause fix: capture the referring NPI when the imaging is ordered/scheduled — not after the denial. A front-end checklist for advanced imaging (auth + referring NPI + diagnosis) prevents this entire class of denial.
questions.hint: When is the cheapest moment to capture the referring NPI?

questions.q: A coworker suggests appealing the original CO-16 denial 'to be safe' alongside the corrected claim. Why is this wrong?
options: Appeals are only for large balances
It creates a duplicate — the corrected claim already resolves it; parallel appeal + correction risks a CO-18 duplicate denial
Appeals take too long
CO-16 denials can't be appealed at all
questions.explanation: Corrected claim and appeal are alternative paths — running both creates duplicates (CO-18) and confusion. CO-16 = correct and resubmit. Appeals are for when the payer's decision was wrong, not when the claim was incomplete.
questions.hint: Two paths to the same destination = collision.

title: Denial Workup: CO-97 Bundled Services
description: 97110 denied CO-97/M15 — bundled into 99213. Check the NCCI edit, decide if a modifier is legitimate, then choose: corrected claim, appeal, or accept.

questions.q: ERA: 99213 paid $100; 97110 (2 units, no modifier) denied CO-97 + M15. What does this code pair mean?
options: The claim was filed late
The therapy was bundled into the office visit per NCCI edits — paid as part of 99213
The diagnosis doesn't support therapy
The patient owes the full amount
questions.explanation: CO-97 = payment adjusted because the benefit is included in another service; M15 = separately billed services were bundled. NCCI edits bundle 97110 into 99213 when no bypass modifier is present.
questions.hint: CO-97 is always about two services collapsing into one payment.

questions.q: The NCCI edit for 99213 + 97110 has modifier indicator 1. What does indicator 1 allow?
options: The two codes can never be billed together
They can be billed together only with a qualifying modifier (e.g., -59/-XS) when the services are truly distinct
Any modifier bypasses the edit automatically
Indicator 1 means no edit exists
questions.explanation: Indicator 1 = bypassable with a modifier ONLY when documentation supports distinct services. Indicator 0 = never together (drop a line). Indicator 9 = no edit. The modifier must reflect reality, not just unlock payment.
questions.hint: 1 = sometimes, with proof. 0 = never. 9 = no rule.

questions.q: You review the note: the therapy was a separately documented 30-minute session for a different body region, clearly distinct from the E/M. What is the correct action?
options: Accept the bundling — write off $135
Appeal with no changes
Submit a corrected claim appending -59 (or -XS) to 97110 with the distinct documentation
Rebill 97110 as 97140 to avoid the edit
questions.explanation: Distinct, documented service = legitimate modifier use. A corrected claim with -59/-XS (check payer preference — Medicare wants X-modifiers) plus the supporting note gets it paid. Recoding to dodge the edit (97140) is abuse.
questions.hint: The documentation supports it — which path uses that documentation?

questions.q: Alternative scenario: the 'therapy' was 5 minutes of range-of-motion during the exam, not separately documented. Now what?
options: Still add -59 — the edit allows it
Accept the bundling; do not append a modifier without distinct documentation
Appeal and hope the payer doesn't check
Bill the patient for 97110
questions.explanation: A modifier certifies the services were distinct — appending it without documentation is false coding and audit exposure. If it wasn't distinct, the bundling is correct: accept it and educate the provider on documentation.
questions.hint: Modifiers attest to facts. What if the fact isn't true?

questions.q: Which of these is NEVER an acceptable way to 'fix' a CO-97 denial?
options: Corrected claim with a supported modifier
Appeal with documentation showing distinct services
Changing the CPT to a code without an NCCI edit to get paid
Accepting the bundling when services weren't distinct
questions.explanation: Recoding to dodge an edit (e.g., 97110 → 97140) without a clinical reason is upcoding/abuse — it misrepresents what was done. All other options are legitimate depending on the documentation.
questions.hint: One of these changes what the claim SAYS happened.

title: Denial Workup: CO-18 Duplicate Claim
description: A $200 claim denied CO-18 — duplicate. The biller wants to rebill 'to be sure.' Investigate the original claim's status first. (Never resubmit a duplicate.)

questions.q: ERA: 99214, billed $200, paid $0, CO-18. What is the FIRST thing to check before doing anything?
options: The patient's eligibility
The status of the original claim — is it paid, pending, or denied?
Whether the CPT code is correct
The timely filing limit
questions.explanation: CO-18 means the payer already has this claim on file. The entire workup hinges on the original's status: paid = done; pending = wait; denied = work the ORIGINAL denial. Acting without this fact risks making things worse.
questions.hint: Duplicate of WHAT? Find the original first.

questions.q: You check: the original claim (same CPT, DOS, patient) shows PAID $180 two weeks ago. What do you do with the CO-18 denial?
options: Resubmit — maybe the payment was a mistake
Appeal the CO-18
Nothing — the claim already paid; close the duplicate as informational
Bill the patient the $20 difference
questions.explanation: Paid is paid — the duplicate denial is just the payer telling you 'we already handled this.' Close it. Resubmitting a paid claim creates more duplicates; appealing a correct denial wastes everyone's time.
questions.hint: The money already arrived. What problem remains?

questions.q: Different scenario: the original claim shows DENIED CO-96 (non-covered). The biller already sent a second identical claim, which denied CO-18. What went wrong?
options: Nothing — rebilling was the right move
The biller worked the duplicate instead of the original denial; the CO-96 on the original was never addressed
The second claim should have had a modifier
CO-18 should have been appealed
questions.explanation: Classic error: chasing the CO-18 instead of the CO-96. The real issue is on the ORIGINAL claim (non-covered charge) — that needs the workup (diagnosis? corrected claim? appeal?). The duplicate is a symptom of impatience.
questions.hint: Which denial has the actual clinical/billing issue?

questions.q: The original claim shows PENDING at the payer for 25 days. The duplicate denied CO-18. Correct action?
options: Resubmit a third time to push it through
Call the payer for a status check on the ORIGINAL claim; do not resubmit
Write off the balance
Appeal the CO-18 denial
questions.explanation: Pending = the payer is still processing. A status call (get a trace/reference number) is the move. Resubmitting while one is pending guarantees another CO-18 and can even slow the original.
questions.hint: The claim is alive at the payer. What do you do with a live claim?

questions.q: True or false: 'When in doubt, rebill — the payer will sort it out.'
options: True — payers deduplicate automatically with no harm
False — blind rebilling creates CO-18s, muddies the audit trail, and can reset timely-filing confusion
True — but only for claims under $100
False — rebilling is illegal
questions.explanation: Blind rebilling is one of the most common rookie mistakes. Every resubmission should be intentional: corrected claim (new info), appeal (dispute), or status check (pending). 'Just rebill' creates the very duplicates you're then forced to work.
questions.hint: Think about what the audit trail looks like after 4 identical claims.

title: Denial Workup: MA130 Unprocessable — New Claim, Not Appeal
description: A claim rejected MA130 — unprocessable as submitted. The biller drafted an appeal letter. Stop: MA130 needs a brand-new claim, and appeals are the wrong tool.

questions.q: Remittance: 99213, billed $150, paid $0, MA130 — 'Claim unprocessable.' How is this different from a denial?
options: It isn't — unprocessable and denied mean the same thing
Unprocessable means the claim couldn't be adjudicated at all (bad data/format); a denial is a judged decision on a clean claim
MA130 is just a slower denial
Unprocessable claims auto-reprocess in 30 days
questions.explanation: Unprocessable = the payer's system couldn't even read/adjudicate it (missing/invalid required data). A denial = the claim was clean enough to judge, and the judgment was no. This distinction dictates the fix.
questions.hint: Can you appeal a decision that was never made?

questions.q: The biller drafted an appeal letter for the MA130. Why is an appeal the wrong move?
options: Appeals are only for claims over $1,000
An appeal disputes a decision — but no decision was made; the claim needs to be fixed and sent as a NEW claim
MA130 appeals are illegal
Appeals take longer than new claims
questions.explanation: Appeals argue 'your decision was wrong.' With MA130 there WAS no decision — the claim never entered adjudication. The fix is a new, clean claim with the missing/invalid data corrected. Filing an appeal wastes the appeal window on a non-decision.
questions.hint: What exactly would the appeal letter be arguing against?

questions.q: Common MA130 triggers include:
options: High billed amounts
Missing/invalid NPI, invalid diagnosis code format, missing required fields — data the payer needs to process the claim
Using modifier -25
Filing on a Friday
questions.explanation: MA130 fires on structural defects: bad NPI, malformed ICD (e.g., missing decimal), blank required fields. The claim-scrubber rules (NPI-001, DX-002, MISS-001) exist precisely to catch these BEFORE submission.
questions.hint: What would stop a computer from even reading the claim?

questions.q: You fix the invalid diagnosis code and submit a new claim. It processes and pays. What happens to timely filing?
options: The new claim gets a fresh filing deadline from today
The ORIGINAL submission date usually counts if you can prove it — keep the clearinghouse acceptance of the first submission
Timely filing no longer applies to new claims
You must appeal to preserve the filing date
questions.explanation: Keep proof of the original transmission (clearinghouse 999/acceptance). Most payers honor the original filing date for a corrected/new claim fixing an unprocessable submission — but only if you can prove when it first went out. This is why transmission logs matter.
questions.hint: The payer rejected the DATA, not the TIMING. What proves the timing?

questions.q: Which scrubber discipline would have prevented this MA130 entirely?
options: Filing claims faster
Pre-submission validation: NPI format, ICD-10 format, required fields, diagnosis pointers — every MA130 trigger is a scrubber rule
Using a different clearinghouse
Adding more diagnosis codes
questions.explanation: Every MA130 cause maps to a scrubber check. The Claim Scrubber lab's rules (NPI-001/002, DX-001/002, MISS-001/002/003) are literally the MA130 prevention kit. Clean-claim rate is the KPI that measures this discipline.
questions.hint: The scrubber lab was built for exactly this.

title: Telehealth Basics: Video Visit Billing
description: A 99213 video visit — code it right with modifier 95 and POS 02, and understand why the payment differs from in-person.

questions.q: Dr. Lee does a 99213-level video visit with an established patient. What is the correct coding?
questions.explanation: Modifier 95 identifies the service as synchronous telehealth; POS 02 tells the payer the patient was at home via telehealth. Together they trigger the telehealth payment rules.
questions.hint: Which modifier means 'via telehealth'? Which POS means 'patient at home on video'?

questions.q: Why does POS 02 typically pay LESS than POS 11 for the same 99213?
options: Telehealth is always considered lower quality
POS 02 pays the facility rate — it assumes lower practice overhead (no exam room, no in-person staff costs)
It is a penalty for using video
POS 02 claims are always denied
questions.explanation: POS 02 reimburses at the facility rate, reflecting lower overhead for the distant-site provider. The payment difference is about practice expense, not quality.
questions.hint: Think about what costs less when the patient is not in the office.

questions.q: The visit was video. A biller codes 99213 with POS 11 (office) and no modifier. What is the compliance risk?
options: None — POS does not matter
Overpayment: POS 11 pays the higher non-facility rate, so the practice is paid more than the telehealth rate allows — an overpayment the payer can recoup
Underpayment only — no compliance issue
The claim will just pend for review
questions.explanation: Coding a telehealth visit as in-person (POS 11, no 95) yields the higher non-facility payment the practice did not earn. Payers treat this as incorrect billing subject to recoupment and audit.
questions.hint: Which direction does the money error go?

questions.q: Which statement about telehealth coverage is TRUE?
options: No payers restrict telehealth — it is universally covered identically to in-person
Coverage varies by payer: some commercial payers limit eligible codes, require specific modifiers (95 vs GT), or exclude certain services — always verify the payer's telehealth policy
Only Medicare restricts telehealth
Only Medicaid restricts telehealth
questions.explanation: Telehealth coverage is payer-specific. Medicare has its telehealth list; commercial payers each publish their own policies with different modifiers, POS rules, and covered codes. Never assume — check the payer policy.
questions.hint: Is telehealth policy the same everywhere?

title: Telehealth vs In-Person: Payment Matters
description: Same CPT, different POS — see exactly how 99213 pays at POS 11 vs POS 02, and when the setting changes the code choice.

questions.q: Fee schedule: 99213 non-facility (POS 11) = $92.47; facility (POS 02/21) = $66.32. A video visit is coded 99213-95, POS 02. What pays?
options: $92.47 — telehealth always pays the office rate
$66.32 — POS 02 triggers the facility rate
$0 — telehealth 99213 is not covered
$79.40 — the average of the two rates
questions.explanation: POS 02 = facility rate ($66.32). The ~$26 difference is the practice-expense reduction for telehealth. Billers must set expectations: telehealth volume needs to account for lower per-visit revenue.
questions.hint: Which rate does POS 02 trigger?

questions.q: A patient has a video visit in the morning (99213-95, POS 02) and comes into the office that afternoon for a wound check (99212, POS 11). How should this be billed?
options: Bill both — they are separate encounters with different POS
Bill only the in-person visit — telehealth and office on the same day always bundle
Bill only the video visit — it happened first
Combine into one 99214
questions.explanation: Separate encounters, separate POS, medically distinct reasons — both are billable. Same-day telehealth + in-person is allowed when each is a separately identifiable service; document both encounters clearly.
questions.hint: Are these the same encounter or two distinct ones?

questions.q: The biller considers adding modifier 25 to the afternoon 99212 because the morning was telehealth. Is modifier 25 needed?
options: Yes — always use 25 for same-day services
No — modifier 25 is for significant separately identifiable E/M on the same day as a procedure; these are two E/Ms at different POS, not E/M + procedure
Yes — telehealth always requires 25
No — same-day services can never both be billed
questions.explanation: Modifier 25 applies when an E/M is significant and separately identifiable from a procedure on the same day. Two E/Ms at different places of service do not need 25 — the different POS already distinguishes them.
questions.hint: What is modifier 25 actually for?

questions.q: For revenue planning: a practice shifts 30% of 99213 volume to telehealth. What should finance expect?
options: Same revenue — telehealth pays identically
Lower per-visit revenue (~28% less per 99213 at facility vs non-facility rates) — offset by higher volume/lower overhead
Higher revenue — telehealth has bonus payments
No way to estimate
questions.explanation: ($92.47 - $66.32) / $92.47 = ~28% less per visit. Telehealth economics work through volume, reduced no-shows, and lower overhead — not per-visit rate. Finance must model the mix shift.
questions.hint: Do the math on the two rates.

title: Audio-Only Telehealth: Modifier 93
description: When video is not possible — audio-only visits with modifier 93, payer restrictions, and documentation requirements.

questions.q: A patient has no smartphone/computer — only a landline. Dr. Patel does a 99213-level visit by phone. What is the correct coding?
options: 99213-95, POS 02 — audio counts as telehealth the same as video
99213-93, POS 02 — modifier 93 specifically identifies audio-only telehealth
99441 — telephone E/M codes are always used instead
99213, POS 11 — just bill it as a regular visit
questions.explanation: Modifier 93 = audio-only telehealth (created to distinguish from audio-video modifier 95). Many payers cover audio-only only for specific codes and populations — 95 and 93 are not interchangeable.
questions.hint: There is a dedicated modifier for audio-only.

questions.q: Which statement about payer coverage of audio-only (93) is TRUE?
options: All payers cover audio-only identically to video
Coverage is payer-specific and often narrower: some payers limit audio-only to certain codes, require patient attestation that video was unavailable, or do not cover it at all
Medicare never covers audio-only
Audio-only always pays more than video
questions.explanation: Audio-only coverage is the most variable corner of telehealth policy. Some payers require documented patient inability to use video; others restrict the code set. Verify per payer, per code.
questions.hint: Is audio-only treated the same as video everywhere?

questions.q: Documentation for the audio-only visit must include:
options: Nothing special — document like any visit
That the visit was audio-only, why video was not available/used, patient consent for telehealth, and start/stop times
Only the diagnosis
A recording of the call
questions.explanation: Audio-only documentation must establish: modality (audio-only), reason video was not used, patient consent, and time (many audio-only codes are time-based). Auditors target audio-only claims — documentation is the defense.
questions.hint: What would an auditor ask about an audio-only claim?

questions.q: The biller used 99441 (telephone E/M, 5-10 min) for a 25-minute audio-only visit that met 99213 MDM. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — telephone codes are preferred
Undercoding: if the visit meets office/outpatient E/M requirements via audio-only, 99213-93 (not 99441) captures the work; 99441 is for brief telephone E/M that does not meet O/O E/M criteria
Overcoding — should be 99442
99441 and 99213-93 pay the same, so it does not matter
questions.explanation: 99441-99443 are for telephone E/M that does NOT meet office/outpatient visit requirements. A full 99213-level audio-only visit is coded as 99213-93. Using 99441 undervalues the service significantly.
questions.hint: Do telephone codes and O/O E/M codes describe the same service?

title: Telehealth + In-Person Same Day: Complex
description: Morning video visit, afternoon procedure — modifier logic, POS combinations, and avoiding unbundling traps.

questions.q: Morning: video visit 99213-95 (POS 02) for knee pain. Afternoon: patient comes in, Dr. Kim does 20610 (knee injection, POS 11). The morning E/M was significant and separately identifiable from the injection decision. Correct billing?
options: 99213 (POS 02) + 20610 (POS 11) — no modifiers needed
Only 20610 — the E/M bundles into the procedure
questions.explanation: Modifier 25 goes on the E/M (99213-95-25), never on the procedure. The 95 stays (telehealth), 25 is added to show the E/M was significant/separately identifiable from the same-day procedure. Different POS further supports separateness.
questions.hint: Which code gets modifier 25 — the E/M or the procedure?

questions.q: What if the morning video visit was ONLY to evaluate whether the injection was needed, and the injection was then done that afternoon?
